title: Memory
theory: An address is not the value
A pointer stores an address. Dereferencing accesses the object at that address. Copying a pointer copies the address, not an independent copy of the underlying object.
Dynamic allocation reserves storage at runtime. Check allocation failure, respect the allocated size, and free owned storage once it is no longer needed. Do not access it after freeing it.
Text copying must account for the null terminator. Know whether a buffer is writable, how large it is, and how long its lifetime lasts. A pointer to a local variable cannot outlive that variable.
Behavior tests are not a memory proof

A program may print the right value while accessing invalid memory. The checker supports an optional sanitizer mode when your C compiler supports it. Record sanitizer results and review ownership explicitly; passing output cases alone is not a memory-safety certificate.

quiz.prompt: int x=5; int *p=&x; *p=10; What is x?
quiz.explanation: p points to x, so writing through p changes x.

quiz.prompt: After q=p, do p and q normally refer to independent copies?
options: No, they hold the same address
quiz.explanation: Pointer assignment does not duplicate the pointed-to object.

quiz.prompt: After free(p), which is valid without a new allocation?
quiz.explanation: The previous allocation is no longer available to access.

quiz.prompt: A copy of a 5-character C string needs at least how many bytes?
Correct output on four inputs proves absence of all memory bugs?
quiz.explanation: Output checks cover observed behavior, not every possible memory error.
